title: The Mool Mantar at the summit
word: The Mool Mantar at the summit
hookLine: the words from day four, now understood
tomorrow: the Japji's first seven pauris, read whole. what holds them together?

lines: THE FIRST WORDS ON THE PATH.
cards: A song you knew as a kid can hit differently years later. Same words, same tune, and one line you used to sing without thinking suddenly sounds like it's about you. The Mool Mantar works like that.
It was among the first words on this path, at the top of the Granth's first page. The words haven't moved. So, at the start of the summit: do they sound the same now?

teach.b: Say it slowly and listen to how it's built. Ik oankaar: One, written as a numeral, joined to the sound Oankar. Sat naam: truth is the name.
Kartaa purakh: the creator, the being who makes.
Nirbhau, nirvair: without fear, without hate. Akaal moorat: a form beyond time. Ajoonee, saibhan: unborn, self-existent.
Gur prasaad: known by the Guru's grace. Macauliffe's translation opens it this way: "There is but one God whose name is true, the Creator." Now listen to the sound.
The middle runs on short, firm words, nirbhau, nirvair, almost like footsteps. The end softens: gur prasaad, by grace, an open hand after all that description.

teach.h: A YEAR LIVED FILLS THEM IN.
teach.b: A year lived has filled those words in. Nirbhau, without fear: Guru Tegh Bahadur walking to Delhi himself. Nirvair, without hate: a Nawab from another faith speaking up for two boys.
Kartaa purakh: a harvest at Vaisakhi. And gur prasaad: a lamp lit at the door for someone coming home. Nothing new is added at the summit.
The first words, said slowly enough to hear what they've been holding all along.

how: The Mool Mantar opens the Guru Granth Sahib and the Japji; Sikhs recite it in the morning prayers, and families often teach it to children first, sometimes saying it slowly together, phrase by phrase.

games.q: what does “the mool mantar at the summit” mean?
o: the closing hymn sung after the whole Japji
a new prayer written for the end of the path
the opening words, said again with a year behind

games.q: the root words — tap the pairs.

s: the Mool Mantar is a beginner's summary you outgrow
the summit opens with it: the same words, deeper, heard with a year behind them.
Macauliffe renders its opening: There is but one God whose name is true, the Creator
from his translation of the Japji, in The Sikh Religion.
it ends on gur prasaad, by the Guru's grace
after every description of the One, the last word is grace.

games.q: a friend says the Mool Mantar is beginner stuff; at the end of a path you should move on to harder texts. what fits today?
o: the same words go deeper; that's why the summit opens with them.
she's right: it's a summary for newcomers, and the summit is elsewhere.
it's only said at the start of the Japji, never on its own.
games.why: nothing new is added at the summit: the first words, said slowly, filled in by a year of living them.

practice: Say the Mool Mantar out loud, as slowly as you can, one phrase for each breath: ik oankaar, sat naam, kartaa purakh, nirbhau, nirvair, akaal moorat, ajoonee, saibhan, gur prasaad.
If the Gurmukhi is new to you, say the English instead: One, truth, creator, without fear, without hate, timeless, unborn, self-existent, grace. Then go round once more, slower.

wordCard.voice: The Mool Mantar at the summit. The Granth's opening words, said again at the top of the path, and heard with a year behind them.

orig.note: Punjabi: the root mantra, the opening words of the Guru Granth Sahib.

carryVoice: Carry this: the same words, deeper, because the one saying them has changed. Day one of the summit.
